chapterNote: The turning point, and it hinges on nothing anyone planned: the king cannot sleep. The chronicles are read, Mordecai's forgotten rescue surfaces, and Haman — arriving at that exact moment to ask for Mordecai's death — is trapped by his own vanity into designing Mordecai's honor and then leading his enemy's horse through the streets. Not a single miracle is named, yet every coincidence leans one direction. Even Haman's household can read it: 'you will surely fall before him.'

1.text: That night sleep fled from the king, so he ordered the book of records, the chronicles, to be brought, and it was read before him.
1.amp: on that night the king's sleep fled [nadedah shenat hammelekh — his sleep escaped him]; and he ordered the book of memorable deeds, the chronicles, to be brought.
1.notes: The quiet fulcrum of the book. Of all nights, the king cannot sleep; of all scrolls, the chronicles are read; of all entries, they land on Mordecai. No angel appears, no voice speaks — only an insomniac king and a well-timed page. This is providence in its most hidden and most unmistakable form.

2.text: There it was found written how Mordecai had exposed Bigthana and Teresh, two of the king's eunuchs, keepers of the threshold, who had plotted to lay hands on King Ahasuerus.

3.text: "What honor or distinction has Mordecai been given for this?" the king asked. "Nothing has been done for him," his attendants answered.

4.text: "Who is in the court?" the king asked. Now Haman had just come into the outer court of the palace to speak to the king about hanging Mordecai on the gallows he had prepared for him.
4.notes: The timing is exquisite. Haman arrives to demand a death at the very hour the king is looking for a way to reward the intended victim. He walks in to ask for Mordecai's gallows and walks out having glorified him.

5.text: "Haman is standing in the court," the attendants said. "Bring him in," said the king.

6.text: When Haman entered, the king asked him, "What should be done for the man the king delights to honor?" And Haman said to himself, "Whom would the king wish to honor more than me?"
6.notes: Dramatic irony at its peak: Haman can imagine no honoree but himself, and so lavishes on his enemy the very tribute he craved. Pride writes its own humiliation, certain the reward is coming home to itself.

7.text: So Haman said to the king, "For the man the king delights to honor,

8.text: let them bring a royal robe the king himself has worn, and a horse the king has ridden, with a royal crest set on its head.

9.text: Let the robe and the horse be handed to one of the king's most noble officials, and let them robe the man the king delights to honor and lead him on horseback through the city square, proclaiming before him, 'This is what is done for the man the king delights to honor!'"

10.text: "Hurry," the king said to Haman, "take the robe and the horse, just as you have said, and do all this for Mordecai the Jew, who sits at the king's gate. Leave out nothing of all you have spoken."
10.notes: One sentence undoes him. 'Mordecai the Jew' — the man Haman meant to impale — must now be robed and paraded by Haman's own hand, and Haman may omit nothing of the honor he so lovingly imagined for himself.

11.text: So Haman took the robe and the horse, robed Mordecai, and led him on horseback through the city square, proclaiming before him, "This is what is done for the man the king delights to honor!"

12.text: Afterward Mordecai returned to the king's gate. But Haman hurried home, grieving, with his head covered.

13.text: And he told his wife Zeresh and all his friends everything that had happened to him. Then his advisers and his wife Zeresh said to him, "If Mordecai, before whom you have begun to fall, is of Jewish descent, you will not prevail against him — you will surely fall before him."
13.notes: Even Haman's own household now recites his doom like an oracle. 'Begun to fall' — the descent has already started, and there is no arresting it. Those who set themselves against this hidden-guarded people are, in the end, read their sentence by their own friends.

14.text: They were still speaking with him when the king's eunuchs came and rushed Haman away to the banquet Esther had made ready.
